text: Spencer Perceval (1 November 1762 – 11 May 1812) was a British statesman and barrister who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from October 1809 until his assassination in May 1812. He is the only British prime minister to have been assassinated and the only solicitor-general or attorney-general to have become prime minister. The younger son of The Earl of Egmont, an Anglo-Irish earl, Perceval was educated at Harrow School and Trinity College, Cambridge. He studied law at Lincoln's Inn, practised as a barrister on the Midland circuit, and became a King's Counsel in 1796. He entered politics at age 33 as a member of Parliament (MP) for Northampton. A follower of William Pitt the Younger, Perceval described himself as a "friend of Mr. Pitt" rather than a Tory; he opposed Catholic emancipation and parliamentary reform, supported the war against Napoleon, and advocated the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade. After a late entry into politics, his rise to power was rapid: he was appointed Solicitor General and then Attorney General for England and Wales in the Addington ministry, Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons in the second Portland ministry, and became prime minister in 1809. At the head of a weak government, Perceval faced crises including an inquiry into the Walcheren expedition, the mental illness of King George III, economic depression, and Luddite riots. He overcame these challenges, successfully pursued the Peninsular War despite opposition defeatism, and won the support of the Prince Regent. His position strengthened by early 1812 when, in the lobby of the House of Commons, he was assassinated by John Bellingham, a merchant with a grievance against his government. Bellingham was hanged one week later. Perceval had four older brothers who survived to adulthood; through the expiry of their male-line heirs, the earldom of Egmont passed to one of his great-grandsons in the early 20th century and became extinct in 2011. Born in Audley Square, Mayfair, London, the seventh son of the 2nd Earl of Egmont, Perceval was the second son of the Earl's second marriage. His mother, Catherine Compton, Baroness Arden, was a granddaughter of the 4th Earl of Northampton. Spencer was a Compton family name; Catherine Compton's great-uncle, Spencer Compton, 1st Earl of Wilmington, had been prime minister. His father, a political adviser to Frederick, Prince of Wales and King George III, served briefly in the cabinet as First Lord of the Admiralty. Perceval's early childhood was spent at Charlton House, London, which his father had taken to be near Woolwich Dockyard. Lord Egmont died when Perceval was eight. He attended Harrow School, where he was disciplined and hard-working, developed an interest in evangelical Anglicanism, and formed a lifelong friendship with Dudley Ryder. After five years at Harrow, he followed his older brother Charles to Trinity College, Cambridge, where he won the declamation prize in English and graduated in 1782. As the second son of a second marriage, Perceval had an annual allowance of £200 and, without inherited wealth, had to establish himself independently. He chose law, studied at Lincoln's Inn, and was called to the bar in 1786. His mother died in 1783. Perceval and his brother Charles, now Lord Arden, rented a house in Charlton, where they fell in love with two sisters from the Percevals' childhood home. The sisters' father, Sir Thomas Spencer Wilson, approved of the match between his eldest daughter Margaretta and Lord Arden, who was wealthy and already a Member of Parliament and a Lord of the Admiralty. Perceval, then an impecunious barrister on the Midland Circuit, was told to wait until the younger daughter, Jane, came of age in three years. When Jane reached 21 in 1790, Perceval's career was still not prospering, and Sir Thomas still opposed the marriage. The couple eloped and married by special licence in East Grinstead. They set up home in lodgings over a carpet shop in Bedford Row, later moving to Lindsey House, Lincoln's Inn Fields. Family connections secured him several positions: Deputy Recorder of Northampton and commissioner of bankrupts in 1790; surveyor of the Maltings and clerk of the irons in the mint—a sinecure worth £119 a year—in 1791; and counsel to the Board of Admiralty in 1794. He acted as junior counsel for the Crown in the trial of Thomas Paine for seditious libel (1792) and the prosecution of John Horne Tooke for high treason (1794). Perceval joined the London and Westminster Light Horse Volunteers in 1794 and served until 1803. He wrote anonymous pamphlets in favour of the impeachment of Warren Hastings and in defence of public order against sedition, which brought him to the attention of William Pitt the Younger. In 1795, he was offered the appointment of Chief Secretary for Ireland, which he declined, as he could earn more as a barrister and needed the money to support his growing family. In 1796, he became a King's Counsel at age 33 and earned about £1,000 a year (equivalent to £124,000 in 2023). In 1796, his uncle, the 8th Earl of Northampton, died. Perceval's cousin Charles Compton, who was MP for Northampton, succeeded to the earldom and took his place in the House of Lords. Perceval was invited to stand for election in his place. In the May by-election, he was elected unopposed. Weeks later, he had to defend his seat in a fiercely contested general election. Northampton had an electorate of about 1,000—every male householder not in receipt of poor relief had a vote—and had a strong radical tradition. Perceval stood for the Castle Ashby interest, Edward Bouverie for the Whigs, and William Walcot for the corporation. After a disputed count, Perceval and Bouverie were returned. Perceval represented Northampton until his death 16 years later, making him the only MP for Northampton to have held the office of prime minister. 1796 was his first and last contested election; in the general elections of 1802, 1806, and 1807, Perceval and Bouverie were returned unopposed. When Perceval took his seat in the House of Commons in September 1796, his political views were already formed. "He was for the constitution and Pitt; he was against Fox and France," wrote his biographer Denis Gray. During the 1796–1797 session, he made several speeches, always reading from notes. His public speaking skills were sharpened at the Crown and Rolls debating society during his law studies. After taking his seat, Perceval continued his legal practice, as MPs did not receive a salary and the House only sat part of the year. During the summer recess of 1797, he was senior counsel for the Crown in the prosecution of John Binns for sedition. Binns, defended by Samuel Romilly, was found not guilty. The fees from his practice allowed him to lease Belsize House in Hampstead. In January 1798, Perceval established his reputation as a debater and future minister with a speech in support of the Assessed Taxes Bill, which aimed to increase taxes on houses, windows, male servants, horses, and carriages to finance the war against France. He used the speech to attack Charles Fox and his demands for reform. Pitt described the speech as one of the best he had ever heard, and later that year Perceval was appointed Solicitor to the Ordnance. Pitt resigned in 1801 when both George III and the Cabinet opposed his bill for Catholic emancipation. As Perceval shared the King's views on Catholic emancipation, he did not follow Pitt into opposition. His career continued to prosper during Henry Addington's administration. He was appointed Solicitor General in 1801 and Attorney General the following year. Perceval did not agree with Addington's general policies (especially on foreign policy) and confined himself to speeches on legal issues. He was retained as Attorney General when Addington resigned, and Pitt formed his second ministry in 1804. As Attorney General, Perceval was involved in the prosecution of radicals Edward Despard and William Cobbett, but also made more liberal decisions on trade unions and improved conditions for convicts transported to New South Wales. When Pitt died in January 1806, Perceval was an emblem bearer at his funeral. Although he had little money (by now he had 11 children), he contributed £1,000 to a fund to pay off Pitt's debts. He resigned as Attorney General, refusing to serve in Lord Grenville's Ministry of All the Talents, as it included Fox. Instead, he became the leader of the Pittite opposition in the House of Commons. During his period in opposition, Perceval used his legal skills to defend Princess Caroline, the estranged wife of the Prince of Wales, during the "delicate investigation." The princess had been accused of giving birth to an illegitimate child, and the Prince of Wales ordered an inquiry, hoping to obtain evidence for a divorce. The government inquiry found the main accusation untrue (the child had been adopted), but criticized the princess's behaviour. The opposition supported her, and Perceval became her adviser, drafting a 156-page letter to King George III in her support, known as The Book. Described by Perceval's biographer as "the last and greatest production of his legal career," Perceval threatened publication of The Book when the King refused to allow Caroline to return to court. However, Grenville's ministry fell again over a difference of opinion with the King on the Catholic question before The Book could be distributed. As a member of the new government, Perceval drafted a cabinet minute acquitting Caroline on all charges and recommending her return to court. He had a bonfire of The Book at Lindsey House, and large sums of government money were spent to buy back stray copies. A few copies remained, and The Book was published soon after his death. On the resignation of Grenville, the Duke of Portland formed a ministry of Pittites and asked Perceval to become Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons. Perceval preferred to remain Attorney General or become Home Secretary and pleaded ignorance of financial affairs. He agreed to the position when the salary (smaller than that of the Home Office) was augmented by the Duchy of Lancaster. Lord Hawkesbury (later Liverpool) recommended Perceval to the King, explaining that he came from an old English family and shared the King's views on the Catholic question. Perceval's youngest child, Ernest Augustus, was born soon after he became Chancellor (Princess Caroline was godmother). Jane Perceval became ill after the birth, and the family moved out of the damp and draughty Belsize House, spending a few months in Lord Teignmouth's house in Clapham before finding a suitable country house in Ealing. Perceval paid £7,500 for the 17th century Elm Grove in 1808 (borrowing from his brother Lord Arden and the trustees of Jane's dowry), beginning the family's long association with Ealing. Meanwhile, in town, Perceval moved from Lindsey House to 10 Downing Street when the Duke of Portland returned to Burlington House. One of Perceval's first tasks as Chancellor was to expand the Orders in Council introduced by the previous administration to restrict neutral trade with France in retaliation to Napoleon's embargo. He also ensured that Wilberforce's bill on the abolition of the slave trade, which had not passed its final stages in the House of Lords when Grenville's ministry fell, would not be rejected in a snap division. Perceval was one of the founding members of the African Institute, established in April 1807 to safeguard the Abolition of the Slave Trade Act. As Chancellor of the Exchequer, Perceval had to raise funds to finance the war against Napoleon. He managed this in his 1808 and 1809 budgets without increasing taxes by raising loans at reasonable rates and making economies. As Leader of the House of Commons, he faced a strong opposition challenging the government on the conduct of the war, Catholic emancipation, corruption, and parliamentary reform. Perceval successfully defended the army's commander-in-chief, the Duke of York, against charges of corruption when the Duke's ex-mistress Mary Anne Clarke claimed to have sold army commissions with his knowledge. Although Parliament voted to acquit the Duke on the main charge, his conduct was criticized, and he accepted Perceval's advice to resign (he was reinstated in 1811). Portland's ministry included three future prime ministers—Perceval, Lord Hawkesbury, and George Canning—as well as two of the 19th century's great statesmen: Lord Eldon and Lord Castlereagh. But Portland was not a strong leader and his health was failing. Political crisis erupted in the summer of 1809 as Canning schemed against Castlereagh, and the Duke of Portland resigned following a stroke. Negotiations began to find a new prime minister: Canning wanted to be either prime minister or nothing; Perceval was prepared to serve under a third person, but not under Canning. The remnants of the cabinet decided to invite Lord Grey and Lord Grenville to form "an extended and combined administration" in which Perceval hoped for the home secretaryship. But Grenville and Grey refused to enter negotiations, and the King accepted the Cabinet's recommendation of Perceval as prime minister. Perceval kissed the King's hands on 4 October and began forming his cabinet. The task was made more difficult because both Castlereagh and Canning had ruled themselves out of consideration by fighting a duel. Having received five refusals for the office, Perceval had to serve as his own Chancellor of the Exchequer—characteristically declining to accept the salary. The new ministry was not expected to last. It was especially weak in the Commons, where Perceval had only one cabinet member—Home Secretary Richard Ryder—and had to rely on backbenchers in debate. In the first week of the new Parliamentary session in January 1810, the government lost four divisions: one on a motion for an inquiry into the Walcheren Expedition (a military force intended to seize Antwerp that instead withdrew after losing many men to an epidemic on the island of Walcheren off the Dutch coast) and three on the composition of the finance committee. The government survived the inquiry into the Walcheren Expedition at the cost of the resignation of its leader, Lord Chatham. The radical MP Sir Francis Burdett was committed to the Tower of London for publishing a letter in William Cobbett's Political Register that denounced the government's exclusion of the press from the inquiry. It took three days, due to various blunders, to execute the warrant for Burdett's arrest. The mob took to the streets in support of Burdett, and troops were called out. As Chancellor, Perceval continued to find funds to finance Wellington's campaign in the Iberian Peninsula while contracting a lower debt than his predecessors or successors. King George III had celebrated his Golden Jubilee in 1809; by the following autumn, he showed signs of a return of the illness that had led to the threat of a Regency in 1788. The prospect of a Regency was unattractive to Perceval, as the Prince of Wales was known to favour Whigs and disliked Perceval for his role in the "delicate investigation." Twice Parliament was adjourned in November 1810 as doctors gave optimistic reports about the King's chances of recovery. In December, select committees of the Lords and Commons heard evidence from the doctors, and Perceval finally wrote to the Prince of Wales on 19 December, saying he planned to introduce a regency bill the next day. As with Pitt's bill in 1788, the bill included restrictions: the regent's powers to create peers and award offices and pensions would be limited for 12 months, Queen Charlotte would be responsible for the King's care, and the King's private property would be managed by trustees. The Prince of Wales, supported by the Opposition, objected to the restrictions, but Perceval steered the bill through Parliament. Everyone expected the Regent to change his ministers, but surprisingly, he chose to retain his old enemy, Perceval. The official reason given by the Regent was that he did not wish to do anything to aggravate his father's illness. The King assented to the Regency Bill on 5 February, the Regent took the royal oath the following day, and Parliament formally opened for the 1811 session. The session was largely occupied by problems in Ireland.

In December, select committees of the Lords and Commons heard evidence from doctors, and Perceval wrote to the Prince of Wales on 19 December stating he planned to introduce a regency bill the next day. Similar to Pitt’s 1788 bill, the regency included restrictions: the regent’s powers to create peers, award offices, and give pensions would be limited for 12 months, Queen Charlotte would oversee the King’s care, and the King’s private property would be managed by trustees. The Prince of Wales, backed by the Opposition, objected to these restrictions, but Perceval successfully pushed the bill through Parliament. Everyone expected the Regent to replace his ministers, but surprisingly, he retained Perceval, citing that he did not wish to do anything that might worsen his father’s illness. The King gave assent to the Regency Bill on 5 February, the Regent took the royal oath the following day, and Parliament formally opened for the 1811 session, which focused on Ireland, the bullion controversy (a bill was passed to make bank notes legal tender), and military operations in the Peninsula. When the regency restrictions expired in February 1812, the King still showed no signs of recovery, and after failing to persuade Grey and Grenville to join the government, the Prince Regent decided to keep Perceval and his ministers. Richard Wellesley, 1st Marquess Wellesley, resigned as foreign secretary following intrigues with the Prince Regent and was replaced by Castlereagh. The opposition intensified its criticism of the Orders in Council, which had caused a crisis with the United States and were blamed for economic depression and unemployment in England; riots erupted in the Midlands and Northern England and were harshly suppressed. Henry Brougham’s motion for a select committee was defeated in the Commons, but under pressure from manufacturers, the government agreed to establish a Committee of the Whole House to examine the Orders in Council and their effects on trade and manufacture, which began hearing witnesses in early May 1812. At 5:15 pm on the evening of 11 May 1812, Perceval was en route to attend the inquiry when a man stepped forward, drew a pistol, and shot him in the chest. Perceval fell to the floor, uttering either “murder” or “oh my God,” which were his last words. He was carried into an adjoining room and propped up on a table with his feet on two chairs, still showing a faint pulse, but when a surgeon arrived, the pulse had stopped and Perceval was declared dead. Initially, it was feared the shooting might signal an uprising, but it soon became clear the assassin—whose actions were unaccompanied by escape—was John Bellingham, a merchant who believed he had been unjustly imprisoned in Russia and was entitled to government compensation, which all his petitions had been rejected. Perceval’s body was laid on a sofa in the speaker’s drawing room and moved to Number 10 in the early hours of 12 May. That morning, an inquest was held at the Cat and Bagpipes public house on the corner of Downing Street, resulting in a verdict of willful murder. Perceval left a widow and 12 children aged between three and 20, and there were soon rumours he had not provided for them adequately; he had only £106 5s 1d in the bank at the time of his death. A few days after his death, Parliament voted to settle £50,000 on his children, with additional annuities for his widow and eldest son. Perceval’s widow married Lieutenant-Colonel Sir Henry Carr in 1815 and was widowed again six years later; she died at age 74 in 1844. Perceval was buried on 16 May 1812 in the Egmont vault at St Luke’s Church, Charlton, London, in a private funeral at her request, with Lord Eldon, Lord Liverpool, Lord Harrowby, and Richard Ryder as pall-bearers. The day before, Bellingham had been tried, refused to plead insanity, and was found guilty, sentenced to death, and executed by hanging on 18 May. Perceval was a small, slight, and very pale man who usually wore black; Lord Eldon referred to him as “Little P.” He never sat for a full-sized portrait; likenesses are either miniatures or based on a death mask by Joseph Nollekens. He was the last British prime minister to wear a powdered wig tied in a queue and knee-breeches in the old-fashioned 18th-century style. He is sometimes called one of Britain’s forgotten prime ministers, remembered mainly for the manner of his death. Though not seen as an inspirational leader, he is generally regarded as devout, industrious, and principled, guiding the country through difficult times despite leading a weak government. A contemporary MP, Henry Grattan, described him using a naval analogy: “He is not a ship-of-the-line, but he carries many guns, is tight-built and is out in all weathers.” Perceval’s modern biographer, Denis Gray, described him as “a herald of the Victorians.” Perceval was mourned by many, including Lord Chief Justice Sir James Mansfield, who wept during his summing up at Bellingham’s trial; however, in some areas, such as Nottingham, crowds following his assassination were in a more cheerful mood. Public monuments to Perceval were erected in Northampton, Lincoln’s Inn, and Westminster Abbey. The Westminster Abbey memorial, by sculptor Richard Westmacott, features an effigy of Perceval with mourning figures representing Truth, Temperance, and Power, and a relief showing the aftermath of the assassination in the House of Commons. Four biographies have been published: Charles Verulam Williams’ work shortly after his death, Spencer Walpole’s biography in 1894, Philip Treherne’s short biography in 1909, and Denis Gray’s 500-page political biography in 1963. Three books have been written about his assassination: one by Mollie Gillen, one by David Hanrahan, and the latest by Andro Linklater entitled Why Spencer Perceval Had to Die. Perceval’s assassination inspired poems such as Universal sympathy on the martyr'd statesman (1812), which reads: “Such was his private, such his public life, That all who differ'd in polemic strife, Or varied in opinion with his plan, Agreed with one accord to love the man.” One of Perceval’s most notable critics, especially on Catholic emancipation, was the cleric Sydney Smith, and in Peter Plymley’s Letters Smith wrote: “If I lived at Hampstead upon stewed meats and claret; if I walked to church every Sunday before eleven young gentlemen of my own begetting, with their faces washed, and their hair pleasingly combed; if the Almighty had blessed me with every earthly comfort–how awfully would I pause before I sent forth the flame and the sword over the cabins of the poor, brave, generous, open-hearted peasants of Ireland!” American historian Henry Adams suggested this image of Perceval remained in Liberal minds for a whole generation. In July 2014, a memorial plaque was unveiled in St Stephen’s Hall of the Houses of Parliament, near where he was killed, proposed by Michael Ellis, Conservative MP for Northampton North (part of which Perceval once represented). In Northampton and Northamptonshire, streets are named in his honour, including Spencer and Percival Streets. Spencer and Jane Perceval had 13 children, of whom 12 survived to adulthood. Four of the daughters never married and lived together throughout their lives; during their mother’s lifetime, they resided in Elm Grove, Ealing, and after her death, moved to Pitzhanger Manor House, while their brother Spencer took over Elm Grove. Cousin marriage was common among the remaining two daughters and two sons.
